evidence.title: Informed Consent for Ambient Documentation Using Generative AI in Ambulatory Care
evidence.outcome: Patient intent to consent under brief vs expanded ambient AI disclosure language
evidence.effect: 84 patients (81.6%) consented with basic information vs 57 (55.3%) when AI features, data storage, and corporate involvement were disclosed; yet 96.1%-98.1% rated data-use details important.
evidence.quote: When provided basic information about the technology ( Figure , A), 84 patients (81.6%) consented; this decreased to 57 patients (55.3%) when details about AI features, data storage, and corporate involvement were disclosed ( Figure , B).

evidence.title: Ethics in Patient Preferences for Artificial Intelligence-Drafted Responses to Electronic Messages
evidence.outcome: Patient reactions to and preferences among AI disclosure wording variants
evidence.effect: Evaluated reactions to disclosure; 893 (61.4%) ranked five disclosure versions; brief statement preferred; disclosure did not greatly reduce satisfaction.
evidence.quote: Participants preferred the shortest disclosure statement, which stated, “This message was written by Dr T. with the support of automated tools,” a takeaway that we are implementing at our health system.

evidence.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence With Youth Codesign to Create Vaping Awareness Advertisements
evidence.effect: No significant association with any of 5 PME measures: χ2 values 0.10 to 4.19; all P > .20.
evidence.quote: Source labeling showed no significant association with PME scores (χ2 values ranging from 0.10 to 4.19; all P > .20).

evidence.title: Key Information Influencing Patient Decision-Making About AI in Health Care: Survey Experiment Study
evidence.outcome: User reactions (credibility, effectiveness, trust, intention to use) to AI disclosure label content
evidence.effect: Provider oversight, regulatory approval, performance, added value improved credibility/effectiveness (OR 1.35-2.05), reduced doubts (OR 0.61-0.77), increased trust/intention to use (OR 1.47-1.73).
evidence.quote: The single profile factorial experiment showed that patients reported good label comprehension, and that information about provider oversight, regulatory approval, device performance, and AI's added value improved perceived credibility and effectiveness of the AI label (odds ratio [OR] range: 1.35-2.05), reduced doubts in the AI device (OR range: 0.61-0.77), and increased trust and intention to use the AI device (OR range: 1.47-1.73).

evidence.title: Influence of believed AI involvement on the perception of digital medical advice
evidence.outcome: Perceived reliability, empathy and willingness to follow advice by labelled source (AI, Human, Human + AI)
evidence.effect: Identical advice labelled AI or Human + AI was rated significantly less reliable and less empathetic than Human-labelled advice. Participants were also less willing to follow it (N = 2,280).
evidence.quote: “AI” and “Human + AI”-labelled advice was evaluated as significantly less reliable and less empathetic compared to “Human”-labelled advice.

evidence.title: Impact of AI-Assisted Diagnosis on American Patients' Trust in and Intention to Seek Help From Health Care Professionals: Randomized, Web-Based Survey Experiment
evidence.outcome: Patient reactions to AI-use disclosure in doctor profile
evidence.effect: Plain disclosure of AI use lowered trust and help-seeking across demographics; trust gap smaller with AI use frequency (β=.09) and larger with self-reported knowledge (β=-.04, P=.08).
evidence.quote: Therefore, merely incorporating AI into medical diagnoses without solid trust-building ethics may inadvertently reduce patient’s trust.

evidence.title: What is Artificial Intelligence (AI) "Empathy"? A Study Comparing ChatGPT and Physician Responses on an Online Forum
evidence.outcome: Effect of perceived AI vs physician authorship label on ratings of empathy, quality, trust
evidence.effect: Responses believed to be physician-authored were rated higher in empathy regardless of actual source (perceived-source main effect ηp2 = 0.17, p < 0.001). Trust ηp2 = 0.25. Disclosure of AI authorship lowered perceived empathy and trust.
evidence.quote: Importantly, having information about who authored the response mattered, as participants rated responses they believed to be from a physician higher in empathy than responses they believed to be generated by a chatbot, regardless of the actual source of the response.

evidence.title: Should AI results be disclosed in mammography reports? A randomised survey study of patient responses to concordant and discordant interpretations
evidence.effect: Discordant AI disclosure reduced trust, 73.0 vs 90.1; p < 0.001, and increased anxiety, 58.0% vs 16.0%; OR = 15.4.
evidence.quote: Disclosure of a discordant AI result significantly reduced trust in the radiologist (73.0 vs 90.1; p < 0.001), and increased anxiety (58.0% vs 16.0%; OR = 15.4), second-opinion intent (50.0% vs 8.7%; OR = 10.2), and legal action consideration (60.7% vs 38.7%; OR = 2.49).

evidence.title: Patient Perceptions and preferences for the disclosure of artificial intelligence generated draft replies to electronic messages - A qualitative study
evidence.effect: GDR disclosure statements elicited concerns about error, authorship, and depersonalization.
evidence.quote: GDR disclosure statements elicited participant concerns about error, authorship, and depersonalization.

evidence.title: Effectiveness of Humanized AI Avatars and Messenger Gender for Dental Postprocedure Instructions: Two Randomized Experiments
evidence.outcome: AI disclosure effects on trust and compliance
evidence.effect: Disclosure effects on following instructions were non-significant; return-to-dentist willingness lower, P<.01, Cohen d=0.35 and 0.37.
evidence.quote: Prior disclosure that the video was AI generated resulted in a lower willingness to return to the same dentist than the real-person condition ( P <.01; Cohen d =0.35 and 0.37 for the disclosed humanized AI and disclosed animated AI conditions, respectively).

commentary.bottom_line: Four studies evaluated patient reactions to AI disclosure content, three of them in simulated settings, and found that wording and length can shift consent, trust, and preference, though one label trial found no effect on perceived message effectiveness. No study compared disclosures designed with human factors or behavioral science input against disclosures designed without it.

perspectives.view: Four studies test the evaluation step, and none tests the design step against a comparator. Three are level 4 simulations and one is a small qualitative deployment study. Results are inconsistent, with two supporting and two null or mixed. Outcomes such as intent and preference are indirect measures of understanding and agency, which supports a rating of very low certainty.

Hazard studies show that plain AI disclosure lowered trust and help-seeking, and that a discordant AI result disclosure raised anxiety from 16.0% to 58.0% (OR 15.4). These studies show the problem exists. One vignette study suggests that adding provider oversight and regulatory approval content may raise trust (OR 1.47-1.73), but no study measured downstream harm.

In the one real deployment, 81.6% of patients consented to ambient AI after brief disclosure, compared with 55.3% after expanded disclosure of features, storage, and corporate involvement. A separate survey found that respondents preferred a brief statement. These findings suggest that disclosure length trades off against uptake, and that testing variants before rollout may reveal this trade-off.

One vignette study of 340 patients focused on racial and ethnic minority respondents and found that oversight and performance content improved credibility (OR 1.35-2.05). No test reported enrolling Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Endorsing sources call for testing with low health literacy users, and the current evidence does not show whether that was done.

One health system evaluated five disclosure versions through an existing patient advisory committee of 1,455 respondents, and 893 (61.4%) completed the ranking task. This suggests that standing advisory panels may offer a low-cost route to reaction testing. No study reported staff time, cost, or the effort of engaging human factors specialists.

In the deployment study, 96.1% to 98.1% of patients rated data-use details important, yet fewer consented when given those details. Portal users in a qualitative study raised concerns about error, authorship, and depersonalization after reading disclosure statements. Patients appear to want the information, and brief wording may withhold content they value.

commentary.research_gap: No trial has compared disclosures developed with human factors or behavioral science input against standard disclosures. None has measured comprehension, decision confidence, perceived burden, or abandonment in live clinical use. Studies of limited English proficiency, low-literacy, Medicaid, and safety-net patients are needed, with follow-up beyond single vignette exposures.
commentary.underserved_note: One simulated study focused on racial and ethnic minority patients. No test reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, so the evidence cannot show whether tested disclosure wording supports understanding for the patients most likely to misread it.
